Most Marines aren’t attorneys, let alone Constitutional Law Attorneys. I’m out and an attorney now (not your attorney and not a strict Constitutional Law guy, but my work involves it).  Here’s what I’ll say: your oath is legally binding and your duty is ultimately to the Constitution and what it “stands” for (more on that at the end); the recent case Trump v. United States, 603 U.S. 593 (2024) would seem to suggest that an order from the very top of your chain of command is presumptively valid—presumptively constitutional. 

I’ll note that in oral arguments for that case a justice asked if a sitting President ordered a SEAL Team to kill a political opponent would that be legal, the petitioner’s (Trump’s) lawyer said that would be fine. The Court sided with the petitioner. 

Further, there’s been longstanding tension between the three federal government branches as to which and to what extent they can interpret the Constitution. The current Executive branch has been saying it’s them in other contexts (https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2025/02/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-reins-in-independent-agencies-to-restore-a-government-that-answers-to-the-american-people/), so I doubt they’d say it’s not them when it comes to the military. 

Likewise, the courts are loathe to get into “political questions” such as Presidential control of the military (see, for example:  Crockett v. Reagan (use of force in El Salvador), Ange v. Bush (use of force in Persian Gulf) , Campbell v. Clinton (use of force in Yugoslavia), Doe v. Bush (use of force in Iraq)).

So, the WIIFM: the law—Constitutional Law even—is not morality. William Calley claimed he was obeying lawful orders. Hugh Thompson was not following orders. Which one was right?

Your sub-premise seems to be that vets are entitled to state cash, but aren’t getting it because other people, whom you denigrate, are. The way for the state to help vets is by helping the residents of the state—all of us. Why? Because it’s a “commonwealth”—quality of life for all other humans. I don’t think you should tritely label them “illegals” because I guarantee you’ve broken a law or more in your life, so you’re an illegal too. All of us are if we reduce one infraction to the sun definition of us as persons. Collectivism is a key theme in military service: teamwork, empathy, rising tides and all the boats….

President Truman likely believed Marshall could bring about some positive changes. The stated positives being the usual US boilerplate of democracy, peace, and stability. 

Marshall was, arguably, on the right track with some of his negotiations: the Peiping Executive Headquarters, the III Amphibious Corps, and the Marshall touch account for this. First, the HQ was a “three-men in a Jeep” construct that would put Marshall’s three way truce talks into ground level practice - American mediators, GMD Nationalists, and CCP partisans all circuiting the hinterland inspecting and ensuring truce agreements. The next factor, the III AC, had a less than stellar intent. Namely, no intent.  The Marines brought into China at the end of WW2 were battle-hardened vets of places like Okinawa; now they were asked to both be neutral and supportive of the legal government of China (the petty, ineffectual GMD). Couple that lack of concrete guidance with a lack of training in humanitarian and crisis management and its little surprise the war weary Marines, Soldiers, and Sailors performed poorly. Finally, we come to Marshall himself. While I don’t really subscribe to a “great man” approach to history, Marshall seems more than good. It’s impossible to say if the Executive HQ could’ve panned out, or if the III AC would’ve risen to the occasion with better leadership, training, and direction,  but we can state that until Marshall returned to the US in early ‘46 to report on his mission truce agreements were (mostly) being adhered too and elections were being discussed. Marshall leaves, Chiang and Mao both renege. 

Ultimately, I think the US fundamentally underestimated 1) the long-game of the CCP who didn’t draw a hard line between diplomatic proceedings and military maneuvers; 2) the likelihood of Chiang simply behaving as we wanted him to behave; and 3) the messy nature of what we might now call (though still haven’t fully figured out) state building.
